title: europes data centre crown is frances lose 2026 08 19
author: Jennifer Johnson
text:
LONDON, Aug 19 (Reuters Breakingviews) - For the past few years, French President Emmanuel Macron has summoned global CEOs to Versailles to win the country a place in their capex plans. But ​developers of AI infrastructure didn’t need much coaxing. This year’s Choose France summit, held in early June, saw Japanese ‌tech investor SoftBank Group (9984.T)
, opens new tab
 pledge up to €75 billion for the construction of new data centres. Meanwhile, Brookfield-owned developer Data4 increased its planned AI-infrastructure spending from €20 billion to as much as €30 billion. Given France’s abundant clean energy and supportive policy environment, promises like these are simple to make – and they might be ​relatively easy to keep.
Last year, the Gallic nation recorded a net electricity-export surplus of 92.3 terawatt hours (TWh) thanks to ​subdued demand and a productive nuclear fleet. The latter factor leaves it in a strong position to ⁠support a major AI infrastructure buildout. RTE, the country’s electricity system operator, has estimated
, opens new tab
 that data centres will use between 15 and 20 ​TWh of electricity in 2030, and between 23 and 28 TWh in 2035. Crucially, the power produced in the country tends to ​be cheaper than that of its powerful neighbours. In the first half of 2025, average French wholesale prices
, opens new tab
 were around $73 per megawatt-hour (MWh) – compared with around $115 per MWh in the UK and just under $100 per MWh in Germany.
It’s therefore not surprising that, even though France has less installed data centre capacity than Germany, ​it led the world last year in terms of foreign direct investment in new projects. Whether it can hang onto its crown ​depends in part on its next government’s attitude towards the tech sector. Macron, who pushed for things like faster construction permits and grid connections, ‌cannot run ⁠in the April 2027 presidential election. However, none of his likely successors have expressed broad-based opposition to new data centre projects.
One exception is left-wing populist Jean‑Luc Mélenchon, who has publicly backed a moratorium on projects serving foreign companies subject to U.S. extraterritorial laws. This concern is more about French technological sovereignty than the resource-use arguments that dominate planning discussions elsewhere in the world. Worries about a digital ​dependence on foreign hyperscalers are growing ​in France, with a July ⁠2026 inquiry by the National Assembly recommending a moratorium on data centre projects that don’t meet sovereignty requirements.
One potential workaround for foreign investors with an eye on the French market is to co-own ​real estate without controlling cloud services or sensitive data. This is the arrangement between France’s Orange ​and New Zealand-based ⁠investor Morrison. The telecoms group is contributing its five French data centres and operating expertise, while Morrison provides debt financing and equity for a €3 billion expansion. With a little ingenuity, and a powerful nuclear energy advantage, France may well become Europe's AI infrastructure winner.
